articles.title: An experiment to glimpse the future Amazon — in pictures
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02909-3David Lapola is testing a big climate-science unknown: how will the forest cope as atmospheric carbon dioxide continues to rise?
articles.content:
From above, the patch of Amazon forest looks like an immense tapestry, full of shades and textures. Rising from the green landscape are metal towers that form six rings above the canopy. It is here, 80 kilometres north of Manaus in Brazil, that David Lapola, a climatologist at the State University of Campinas (Unicamp) in Brazil, and his team come to listen to the forest breathe.

The rings mark the site of the Amazon Free-Air CO 2 Enrichment Experiment (AmazonFACE), which is set to launch in the next few months. The decade-long project will test how the forest might respond to atmospheres of the future, when rising carbon dioxide levels are likely to affect plant growth and carbon storage.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant scientific experiment (AmazonFACE) designed to understand how the Amazon rainforest will respond to rising atmospheric CO2 levels, which has broad implications for climate change mitigation and ecosystem conservation. This research has meaningful potential to inform climate action and environmental policy on a global scale.
articles.personality_title: Scientists launch experiment to see how the Amazon forest will grow with more carbon dioxide
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Amazon rainforest is one of the largest and most important forests in the world. It helps control the Earth's climate by absorbing carbon dioxide (CO2), a gas that contributes to global warming. But scientists do not yet know how the forest will react as CO2 levels keep rising in the future.

**What happened** – A team led by David Lapola at the State University of Campinas in Brazil is starting a new experiment called AmazonFACE. This project uses metal towers arranged in six circles above the forest canopy, about 80 kilometers north of Manaus. These towers release extra CO2 to mimic future atmospheric conditions. The experiment will run for ten years to observe how the Amazon trees and plants grow and store carbon in a higher CO2 environment.

**Impact** – This experiment is unique because it studies the forest in its natural setting, not in a lab. It will help scientists understand if the Amazon can keep absorbing carbon as the world changes. Knowing this is important because the forest’s ability to store carbon affects global climate change. The results could guide better policies to protect the Amazon and fight climate change.

**What’s next step** – Over the next decade, researchers will collect data on how plants respond to the increased CO2. This information will show whether the forest grows faster, stores more carbon, or faces new challenges. It may also inspire similar experiments in other important forests around the world.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new long-term experiment in the Amazon will reveal how rising carbon dioxide levels affect the rainforest’s growth and its role in fighting climate change.

articles.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
articles.summary: Dramatic flames from the huge Cairngorms wildfire in July have disappeared - but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.
articles.content:
It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.

It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.

The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.

But that is exactly what we have come to find.

After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.

"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."

It doesn't take long.

"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.
articles.reasoning: The article describes the innovative use of thermal drones to detect hidden hot spots after a large wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park. This represents a significant technological and environmental effort to manage and mitigate wildfire damage, benefiting the ecosystem and public safety on a meaningful scale. The story provides clear context and details about the ongoing monitoring and recovery process.
articles.personality_title: Drones help find hidden fires under the Cairngorms after wildfire
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In July, a large wildfire burned across the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland. Although the visible flames disappeared, some hot spots kept burning underground, which can be dangerous and hard to detect.

**What happened** – Since the wildfire, drone pilot Pete Short has been flying thermal drones over the park every morning. These drones use special cameras to spot heat beneath the earth, showing areas where fires still burn even if we can’t see smoke or flames.

**Impact** – Using drones in this way helps firefighters and park workers find hidden fires quickly. This is important because underground fires can cause new flames or damage the environment if left unchecked. The technology makes the job safer and more effective.

**What’s next step** – The team will keep flying drones regularly to monitor the park until all the hot spots are fully out. This ongoing work will help the land recover and prevent future wildfires from starting in the same places.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Thermal drones are playing a key role in safely spotting and stopping hidden fires after a major wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des drones détectent les feux cachés sous les Cairngorms après un incendie

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Depuis l’incendie, le pilote de drone Pete Short survole chaque matin le parc avec des drones thermiques. Ces drones utilisent des caméras spéciales pour détecter la chaleur sous la terre, montrant où le feu brûle encore même sans fumée ou flammes visibles.

**Impact** – L’utilisation des drones aide les pompiers et le personnel du parc à trouver rapidement ces feux cachés. C’est important car les feux souterrains peuvent provoquer de nouveaux incendies ou endommager l’environnement s’ils ne sont pas contrôlés. **Prochaine étape** – L’équipe continuera à survoler régulièrement le parc jusqu’à ce que tous les points chauds soient complètement éteints. Ce suivi aide la nature à se rétablir et évite que de nouveaux incendies ne repartent aux mêmes endroits.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les drones thermiques jouent un rôle essentiel pour repérer et arrêter en toute sécurité les feux cachés après un grand incendie dans le parc national des Cairngorms.

**Contexto** – En julio, un gran incendio arrasó el Parque Nacional de Cairngorms en Escocia. Aunque las llamas visibles desaparecieron, algunos puntos calientes siguen ardiendo bajo tierra, lo que puede ser peligroso y difícil de detectar.

articles.title: Chemicals at former fuel depot 'have been removed'
articles.summary: Barrels of forever chemicals left at a development site have been removed, a developer has said.
articles.content:
Barrels of chemicals left at an approved development site have been removed and testing carried out, a developer has said.

The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire is a former RAF and Esso fuel storage and transfer facility and has had outline planning permission approved to build residential and affordable homes.

Concerns were raised after campaigners discovered about 40 barrels of firefighting foam liquid, which contains PFAS - a group of chemicals often dubbed forever chemicals, had been left at the site for decades.

Developer, Newcore, said it had already identified the potential contamination and that "this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately."

The depot previously supplied fuel to the former RAF Upper Heyford, around five miles north, which is suspected to be the source of forever chemical, or PFAS, contamination from firefighting foam.

Images show the barrels to be manufactured by Angus Fire Armour, that settled a legal battle out of court with residents in Yorkshire, after claims they had been exposed to PFAS near the company's foam manufacturing plant.

CEO of Newcore, Hugo Llewelyn, who took over the site in 2012, said it plans to regenerate the site with 50% affordable housing and that it was made aware of the barrels "in recent weeks" and had them removed in a "responsible and professional manner".

"Whilst firefighting foam containers were present on site from the MOD's operation back in the 20th Century, we do not believe it was ever deployed; the containers were sealed; and successive surveys have confirmed that there is no "pathway" for it to cause pollution," he added.

Mr Llewelyn disputes the quality of the testing carried out by campaigners.

"A 'pressure group' has trespassed unlawfully to obtain a questionable sample from this site to demonstrate that in the secured area of the site that was purposefully designed to accommodate foam for firefighting purposes, which is likely to contain PFAS, does, according to their findings, contain PFAS.

"I'm not sure there is anything to be surprised about here," he said.

He added that a Phase 1 assessment of the site last year had already identified the potential for contamination and that, "the specification for the Phase 2 investigation has therefore been designed to specifically address this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately".

The Environment Agency's Chemical Compliance team had contacted the site owners to ensure that the drums are properly managed.
articles.reasoning: The article reports the removal of hazardous 'forever chemicals' barrels from a former fuel depot site, addressing contamination concerns and enabling safe redevelopment with affordable housing. This represents meaningful environmental remediation and community benefit, with clear details on the cleanup and future plans.
articles.personality_title: Barrels of harmful chemicals safely removed from former fuel depot in Oxfordshire
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire was once used by the RAF and Esso to store and transfer fuel. The site has planning approval to build new homes, including affordable housing. 

**What happened** – About 40 barrels containing firefighting foam with PFAS chemicals, sometimes called forever chemicals, were found at the site. These barrels had been left there for decades. The developer, Newcore, discovered the barrels recently and removed them carefully. They also tested the site to check for contamination.

**Impact** – Removing these barrels is important because PFAS chemicals do not break down easily and can harm the environment and people’s health. The cleanup makes the land safer for building homes. Newcore plans to include 50% affordable homes, helping local families.

**What's next step** – Newcore will continue testing the site to find any remaining contamination and clean it up if needed. The Environment Agency is monitoring the cleanup to make sure it follows safety rules. Once the site is safe, construction of homes can move forward.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Harmful PFAS chemical barrels have been removed from a former fuel depot, allowing safe development of new affordable housing in Oxfordshire.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des barils de produits chimiques dangereux retirés en toute sécurité d'un ancien dépôt de carburant dans l'Oxfordshire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le dépôt de carburant d'Islip dans l'Oxfordshire était autrefois utilisé par la RAF et Esso pour stocker et transférer du carburant. Le site a obtenu l'autorisation de construire de nouveaux logements, dont des logements abordables.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Environ 40 barils contenant de la mousse anti-incendie avec des produits chimiques PFAS, parfois appelés produits chimiques éternels, ont été découverts sur le site. Ces barils y étaient depuis des décennies. Le promoteur, Newcore, a récemment découvert les barils et les a retirés avec soin. Ils ont également testé le site pour vérifier la contamination.

**Impact** – Retirer ces barils est important car les produits chimiques PFAS ne se décomposent pas facilement et peuvent nuire à l'environnement et à la santé. Le nettoyage rend le terrain plus sûr pour construire des maisons. Newcore prévoit d'inclure 50 % de logements abordables, aidant ainsi les familles locales.

**Prochaine étape** – Newcore continuera à tester le site pour détecter toute contamination restante et la nettoiera si nécessaire. L'Agence de l'environnement surveille le nettoyage pour s'assurer qu'il respecte les règles de sécurité. Une fois le site sécurisé, la construction des logements pourra avancer.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Des barils de produits chimiques PFAS dangereux ont été retirés d'un ancien dépôt de carburant, permettant un développement sûr de nouveaux logements abordables dans l'Oxfordshire.
articles.personality_title_es: Barriles de productos químicos peligrosos retirados con seguridad de un antiguo depósito de combustible en Oxfordshire
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El depósito de combustible Islip en Oxfordshire fue usado por la RAF y Esso para almacenar y transferir combustible. El sitio tiene permiso para construir nuevas viviendas, incluyendo viviendas asequibles.

**Qué pasó** – Se encontraron unos 40 barriles con espuma contra incendios que contienen productos químicos PFAS, conocidos como químicos eternos, que habían estado en el lugar durante décadas. El desarrollador, Newcore, descubrió los barriles recientemente y los retiró con cuidado. También hicieron pruebas para detectar contaminación.

**Impacto** – Retirar estos barriles es importante porque los químicos PFAS no se descomponen fácilmente y pueden dañar el medio ambiente y la salud humana. La limpieza hace que el terreno sea más seguro para construir viviendas. Newcore planea que el 50 % de las casas sean asequibles, ayudando a familias locales.

**Próximo paso** – Newcore seguirá haciendo pruebas para encontrar cualquier contaminación restante y la limpiará si es necesario. La Agencia de Medio Ambiente supervisa la limpieza para asegurar que se sigan las normas de seguridad. Cuando el sitio sea seguro, se podrá continuar con la construcción.

**Resumen en una frase** – Barriles con químicos PFAS peligrosos fueron retirados de un antiguo depósito de combustible, permitiendo el desarrollo seguro de nuevas viviendas asequibles en Oxfordshire.
